opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to separate two things people mix up when they say "multimodal scaling." One is adding more modalities, like images, audio, and video, on top of a language model. The other is scaling on signals that go well beyond what humans have already written down. My honest view is that the first gives real but fairly bounded gains, and the second is where the more interesting intelligence gains might come from.

On the first: adding vision or audio clearly makes models more useful. They can read a chart, follow a video, hear tone in a voice. But if you look at core reasoning, how well the model plans, abstracts, and solves something new, the gains from piling on multimodal data have been smaller than many people expected. A lot of the "intelligence" in these systems still seems to come from language, because language is already a highly compressed record of human thinking. Pixels are rich but redundant. You spend a lot of compute to recover structure that text gives you almost for free.

So when people ask whether multimodal scaling will deliver the next big jump in intelligence, I'm cautious. I don't think simply feeding in ten times more video gets you a qualitatively smarter model. It gets you a model that perceives the world better, which matters, but perception and reasoning aren't the same thing.

What excites me more is the "far beyond" part: scaling on data the model generates through interaction. When a model acts in an environment, writes code and runs it, tries a proof and gets checked, or uses tools and sees the result, it gets feedback that isn't just imitation of humans. That's where I think you can push past the ceiling of human-written data. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has already shown this in math and coding. The open question is how far it generalizes to messier domains where "correct" is harder to define.

If I had to put it in one sentence: multimodality widens what the model can see, but interaction and feedback are what deepen how it thinks. Long term, I expect the biggest gains where the two meet, models that perceive the physical or digital world and also act in it and learn from the consequences. We're still early there, and I'd be skeptical of anyone who claims to know exactly how steep that curve will be.

r001.rationale: The response says multimodal gains have been smaller than expected, but it does not suggest that insufficient compute scaling in language-only and far-beyond-multimodal training explains the lack of strong gains.

r002.rationale: It says video helps models perceive the world better, but does not attribute increased world knowledge to training on video.

r003.rationale: The response offers personal views, but does not characterize the benefits as assessed through subjective firsthand experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm more cautious about this than most people in the field right now.

The intuition everyone has is that if you give the model more modalities, it understands the world more fully, and so it should become smarter. Vision, audio, video, action, all of it. And there's something to that. A model that has seen how objects move, how light behaves, how a voice changes when someone hesitates, has information that pure text simply doesn't carry. Text is a compressed, already-interpreted version of the world. Multimodal data is closer to the raw signal.

But when I actually look at what happened as we scaled multimodal training, the gains in what I'd call core intelligence, reasoning, abstraction, the ability to hold a hard problem and work through it, those gains were much smaller than the gains in perception. The model got dramatically better at seeing and describing. It did not get dramatically better at thinking. Those are different things, and I think we conflated them for a while.

Part of the reason is that most of human intellectual achievement is already encoded in language. Mathematics, science, law, philosophy, we wrote it down. The density of reasoning per token in a good textbook is enormous. The density of reasoning per frame in a video is close to zero. So when you add petabytes of video, you add a lot of signal about the physical world, but very little signal about how to reason. From a pure "intelligence per unit of compute" perspective, it's actually quite expensive.

So where do I think the real gains are? Two places. First, grounding. Language models sometimes say things that are linguistically plausible but physically absurd, and multimodal training genuinely reduces that. It gives the model a sanity check on its own words. Second, and this is the one I'm more excited about, is when the modalities are not just inputs but the medium for action. A model that can look, act, see the result, and adjust is learning from feedback, not just from a static corpus. That's a qualitatively different learning signal, and I think that's where the next real jump in intelligence will come from, not from simply ingesting more pixels.

So my honest assessment: far-beyond-multimodal scaling gives you a much better perceiver and a somewhat better reasoner. If your goal is intelligence specifically, it's necessary but not sufficient, and I'd rather spend the marginal compute on reasoning and on interaction than on a tenth modality.

r001.rationale: The candidate says multimodal data adds little reasoning signal per unit of compute, but does not suggest that too little compute scaling explains why strong intelligence gains have not appeared.

r002.rationale: It says video adds substantial signal about the physical world and describes multimodal training as improving grounding, attributing world-related information to video.

r003.rationale: The candidate frames the assessment as personal judgment, saying, “when I actually look at what happened as we scaled multimodal training” and “my honest assessment.”

astra-6.text:
I’d separate gains in capability from gains in underlying intelligence. A model can handle more modalities and more tasks without necessarily becoming better at reasoning through an unfamiliar problem.

If by “far beyond multimodal scaling” you mean scaling toward richer interaction with the world, then the key question is whether those experiences produce transferable understanding. Can the model use what it learns in one setting to solve a different problem? Can it recognize when its assumptions are wrong and revise them? Can it plan over longer horizons without losing track of the objective?

I’d look for improvements on those dimensions, rather than treating the number of modalities or the volume of training data as evidence by itself. Scaling gives us an opportunity for intelligence gains; whether we’ve achieved them needs to be demonstrated.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling may offer an opportunity for intelligence gains, but does not suggest insufficient compute scaling explains why gains have not been observed.

r002.rationale: It does not mention video training or attribute increased world knowledge to video.

r003.rationale: It proposes evaluating transfer, revision, and planning, but does not characterize perceived benefits as assessed through subjective firsthand experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between broader capability and deeper intelligence. Adding more modalities can give a model a richer understanding of the world, but that alone doesn’t establish that it can reason better, learn more efficiently, or handle unfamiliar situations.

For scaling far beyond that, I’d look at whether the gains transfer: can the model use something it learned in one setting to solve a genuinely new problem? Can it recognize a mistake and revise its approach? Can it sustain coherent reasoning over a longer task?

So I’m open to substantial gains, but I wouldn’t infer them just from the scale of the system. The stronger evidence would be reliable improvements on those abilities, especially where memorization or familiar patterns aren’t enough.
